NIST DLMF §§10.17 and 10.21 fixed-order asymptotic formulas used in the proof
correctness.rationale: Polar radial integration and the Bessel differentiation rule give (2 pi)^(d/2) x^-d [f(x)-f(qx)] with f=x^(d/2)J_(d/2); at zero the volume is positive. From f''+f=(d-1)f'/x, the energy f^2+f'^2 increases strictly in the integral sense. It yields alternating signs of the difference at consecutive extrema and strict |f'(x)|>|f'(qx)| at any zero, so all crossings in a gap have the same orientation and are simple. The first gap before alpha_1 has no root by monotonicity. Implicit differentiation makes q x_n(q) strictly increasing; it tends to 0 at q=0 and alpha_n at q=1 (the limiting sign of F_q/(1-q) at any fixed interior point is the derivative sign, opposite to the sign at the left endpoint). At stationary points q x_n=alpha_m, the second derivative is X^2 f''(alpha_m)/f'(X) and is nonzero. The fixed-order Bessel expansions give alpha_j=pi(j+gamma)+O(1/j), alternating extrema of magnitude proportional to alpha_j^((d-1)/2), and uniform normalized profile cos(pi u)+O(1/n) in the gap. Equating critical heights gives the two parity limits, and expansion of alpha_m/X gives the stated first correction, with a uniform O(1/n) unscaled bound by the gap endpoints. A Riemann sum on each parity away from m/n endpoints suffices for weak convergence, since the omitted fractions can tend to zero. The cosine change of variables gives the stated integrable density and central window law, including epsilon=0 and 1/2. The midpoint behavior and the d=3 reduction follow directly.
residual_risks: The packaged finite distribution and phase comparisons print the differences; some limits have no closeness assertion in those scripts. This is numerical illustration, not evidence of all-index or fixed-d limit validity. The analytic proof is decisive. No uniformity in increasing d is claimed.

value.rationale: The phase law resolves information lost in both the finite census and the uniform unscaled distribution of radii. It supplies a quantitative way to predict where critical zeros accumulate within a Bessel gap, separates the two interleaved sequences and explains the change from suppression in dimension two to an integrable midpoint singularity in dimensions four and above. This is a motivated quantitative asymptotic for a natural family of transforms.
residual_risks: Value concerns this fixed-dimension phase and radius law; the result is not a general optical model or a statement about arbitrary radial profiles.
